title: The origin of turbulence and turbulent diffusivity
status: reviewed and locally validated; passes 1-9 complete; gate 6b passed round 2 (0 blocking)
transcript_provenance: Local machine transcription (faster-whisper small.en); not publisher captions
source_uncertainties: Unverified (named in reader text, not opened): Rayleigh (1880), 'On the stability, or instability, of certain fluid motions'. The derivation (4.3)-(4.5) follows Darrigol (2002, pp. 49-50), who reconstructs Rayleigh's argument; the reader text says so.

Unverified (named in reader text, not opened): Tennekes and Lumley, A First Course in Turbulence (1972), to which the lecture attributes the reading of Re as a ratio of time scales and the judgement that it is more reliable; the chapter attributes both to the lecture and relies on neither.

Slide (L8 f0058) gives 17 cm/s for the kinetic energy g h dtheta/theta = 0.03 m^2/s^2, which equals (g h dtheta/theta)^(1/2); the spoken explanation (L8 1566-1579 s) equates the energy to (1/2)V^2, which gives 0.26 m/s. The chapter states both and the factor sqrt(2).

Slide (L9 f0016, f0040) calls gamma a 'heat conductivity' / 'thermal conductivity'; the quantity in eqs. (1), (4), (9) of the slides is the heat diffusivity (m^2/s). The chapter writes Gamma (NOTATION.md) and says so.
Lecture states Pr = 0.73 for air (L9 f0016); the chapter computes 0.71 at 300 K from the 1976 U.S. Standard Atmosphere formulas and gives both.
Slide Re = 15000 for the room (L9 f0020); with nu = 1.569e-5 m^2/s at 300 K the value is 1.59e4. Both are given.

Lecture-stated values not checked against a primary source: room length 5 m; u ~ 5 cm/s as one third of the plume speed (the lecture's '30 %' fluctuation level); radiator height 0.1 m; dtheta = 10 K; smallest eddies about 1 cm (the lecture defers the estimate to the dissipation equations); roughness making transition occur sooner; laminarization by magnetic fields at low magnetic Reynolds number and by stable stratification; the transition sequence through secondary instabilities and turbulent spots; Re_delta* ~ 600 for the boundary layer and Re_D ~ 2100 for the pipe.

Schubauer and Skramstad Figure 7 (p. 7): the transition Reynolds numbers 2.8e6 (turbulence below about 0.08 %) and 1.5e6 (0.34 %) are read from the graph, not from a table; reading uncertainty about +/-0.1e6.

Reynolds (1883): the critical velocities are given as 1/43.79 and 1/278 times P/D in metre units with P a relative viscosity factor (pp. 943, 948); the chapter uses only their ratio 6.3. Converting either to Re_D would need the viscosity of water at 0 C, which was not checked; Exercise 6 identifies the lower value with ~2000 from Meseguer and Trefethen and says that the combination is the chapter's.

Meseguer and Trefethen (2003): pages checked in the Oxford Research Archive preprint (preprint pp. 1, 4, 10-11, 13, 15-16); journal pagination (J. Comput. Phys. 186, 178-197) not checked. Their Reynolds number definitions for plane Couette and plane Poiseuille flow were not read; Exercise 3 quotes the Couette value 350 as an order of magnitude and says so.

Taylor, 'Diffusion by continuous movements': the PDF pages carry the reading date 10 June 1920; the publication year 1922 is from the Crossref record of DOI 10.1112/plms/s2-20.1.196 (issue s2-20(1), pp. 196-212).

U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976: in the scanned NTRS copy the exponent of the sea-level thermal conductivity in Table 10 (p. 20) reads as 10^-3; eq. (53) gives 2.5326 x 10^-2 W/(m K) at 288.15 K, the value also computed in a reader's errata note appended at PDF p. 243 (which concerns Table III, p. 101). The chapter uses eq. (53) at 300 K, not the table value. c_p = 3.5 R assumes a calorically perfect diatomic gas with the standard's ratio of specific heats 1.40.

The lecture recalls 'Taylor's hypothesis' (module 1) for converting the spatial decay of grid turbulence to a temporal one (L8 514-528 s); the chapter states only the conversion x -> x/U and does not discuss the hypothesis.

The slide figure of the flat-plate boundary layer (L8 f0014) labels the regions 'Low mixing: >> (du/dy)' and 'HIGH mixing (du/dy) >>', and the speech compares du/dy with 1 (L8 333-392 s); du/dy has units 1/s, so the chapter states only that the turbulent profile is fuller with a larger wall gradient. The figure's source (engineersvault.com) is not a primary source and is not cited.

ASR spellings corrected: 'Teneckis and Lumley', 'Ternicus and Lumley', 'Tenkes and Lumley', 'Genesis and Lambda' = Tennekes and Lumley; 'lambda flow' = laminar flow; 'turbula flow' = turbulent flow; 'density defenses' = density differences; 'cube row to the volume of the row' = cube root of the volume of the room; 'New' = nu; 'edit diffusivity' = eddy diffusivity; '100 Hz' = 100 hours; 'turbulent flow in a row' = in a room.
Timestamps are section anchors from local speech-recognition segment times; they locate topic changes to within a few seconds.

sections.section: The objects of the chapter and the running case
sections.lecture_material: Room of size L (cube root of the volume), temperature theta at about 300 K, heat diffusivity (slides gamma), r.m.s. velocity u.
sections.research_extension: U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976: eqs. (51), (53) (p. 19), Table 10 (p. 20), ratio of specific heats 1.40 (p. 18); nu = 1.57e-5 m^2/s, Gamma = 2.22e-5 m^2/s, Pr = 0.71 at 300 K.
sections.teaching_construction: Formal model of the room and its three times; meaning of ~; note on gamma as a diffusivity.

sections.section: Turbulence begins as an instability of a laminar flow
sections.lecture_material: Turbulence arises from instabilities of laminar flow; pipe Re = UD/nu ~ 2100 (roughness makes transition sooner); zero-pressure-gradient boundary layer unstable at U delta*/nu ~ 600; critical Reynolds number.
sections.research_extension: Reynolds 1883 (pp. 943, 946, 948): sensitivity to inlet disturbance, two critical velocities, ratio 278/43.79. Meseguer and Trefethen 2003 (preprint pp. 1, 4, 10-11, 15-16): decaying eigenmodes to R = 1e7, transition depends on nonlinearity, transition near 2000. Schubauer and Skramstad 1948 (pp. 2, 7, 30): instability versus transition, delta* = 1.72 (nu x/U0)^(1/2), lower limit 450, transition at R_x ~ 2.8e6 and 1.5e6 by free-stream turbulence.
sections.teaching_construction: Definitions (4.1); conversion (4.2) of Re_delta* to Re_x; statement that each critical Re belongs to one flow, one length and one disturbance level.

sections.section: Free shear layers can be unstable without viscosity
sections.lecture_material: Free shear flows unstable at very low Re by an inviscid mechanism that does not operate in boundary layers and pipe flow; wall flows have a velocity gradient because of the surface.
sections.research_extension: Darrigol 2002 (pp. 49-50): Rayleigh's 1880 stability equation and inflection-point criterion, eq. (19) vorticity conservation. Blasius 1908 (TM p. 7): zeta zeta'' = -zeta'''. Meseguer and Trefethen 2003 (p. 15): plane Poiseuille eigenvalue instability at R ~ 5772. Schubauer and Skramstad (pp. 1, 30): viscous stability theory of Tollmien and Schlichting, 'good agreement with theory'.
sections.teaching_construction: In-place proof that 2D inviscid vorticity is conserved (curl of the inviscid momentum equation; stretching term zero in 2D); derivation (4.3)-(4.5) in book notation; three-profile check (tanh, Poiseuille, Blasius sign argument); boundary (necessary, inviscid, linear, parallel).

sections.section: Turbulence needs a supply of energy
sections.lecture_material: Turbulence cannot maintain itself; it depends on its environment for energy; shear and buoyancy as common sources.

sections.section: Turbulence begins as an instability of a laminar flow (flat-plate figure, treated in that section)
sections.lecture_material: Figure of a flat-plate boundary layer: laminar region, transition region, turbulent region; low and high mixing; fuller turbulent profile.
sections.research_extension: Schubauer and Skramstad 1948 (pp. 2, 7, 30) for the positions of instability and transition.
sections.teaching_construction: The du/dy labels rendered as a statement about the wall gradient; the figure placed with the Re_delta* to Re_x conversion.

sections.section: Turbulence needs a supply of energy (continued)
sections.lecture_material: Turbulence decays without shear or buoyancy; Re decreases and the flow tends to laminar; decay of grid turbulence; Taylor's hypothesis recalled; laminarization by magnetic fields and stable stratification.
sections.teaching_construction: Room as buoyancy source; switching off the radiator; ceiling heater as stable stratification (illustration).

sections.section: Turbulence begins as an instability of a laminar flow (from instability to developed turbulence, treated in that section)
sections.lecture_material: Transition details poorly understood; primary 2D instability, 3D secondary motions, turbulent spots at random positions and times that grow and merge.
sections.research_extension: Reynolds 1883 (p. 943): eddies appear in a 'full-blown manner'.
sections.teaching_construction: Paragraph placed in the transition section, next to the instability-versus-transition distinction, with its own timestamp anchor (L8 10:24).

sections.section: Without air motion, heat crosses the room in days
sections.lecture_material: Diffusivity as the outstanding characteristic; orders of magnitude faster transfer (fire versus candle flame); imposed-length problem; heat equation (slide eq. 1); Tm ~ L^2/gamma (slide eq. 2); L = 5 m gives order 1e6 s, more than 100 h.
sections.research_extension: Gamma at 300 K from the Standard Atmosphere formulas.
sections.teaching_construction: Numerical value 1.1e6 s; slowest-mode exact solution in an insulated cube, tau_1 = L^2/(pi^2 Gamma) = 32 h; 10 % time 73 h; dependence of the constant on the definition.

sections.section: A weak buoyant stir mixes the room in minutes
sections.lecture_material: Weak buoyant motions disperse heat quickly; Tt ~ L/u (slide eq. 3); buoyant acceleration g dtheta/theta ~ 0.3 m/s^2; KE g h dtheta/theta ~ 0.03 m^2/s^2; 17 cm/s; u ~ 5 cm/s; Tt = 100 s; eddies of about 1 cm smoothed in l^2/gamma, a few seconds.
sections.teaching_construction: sqrt(2) discrepancy between the slide speed and (1/2)V^2; ratio Tm/Tt = 1.1e4 with uncertainty; two-step mechanism (transport by large eddies, molecular smoothing at 1 cm, 4.5 s).

sections.section: A weak buoyant stir mixes the room in minutes (recap)
sections.lecture_material: Recap of the room case: 100 hours versus 2 minutes; 1 cm eddies dissipated in a few seconds; diffusion by random motion very rapid.

sections.section: The ratio of the two times is a Peclet number
sections.lecture_material: Tt/Tm ~ gamma/(uL) = 1/Pe (slide eq. 4); for gases gamma ~ nu, nu/gamma = 0.73 = Pr, so Tt/Tm ~ 1/Re (slide eq. 5); larger Re widens the gap.
sections.teaching_construction: Identity Pe = Pr Re; room values Pe = 1.1e4, Re = 1.6e4; domain limit at Pe ~ 1 (Exercise 1).

sections.section: The ratio of the two times is a Peclet number (Re as a ratio of times)
sections.lecture_material: Re = 15000 in the example; Re as ratio of a turbulence time to a molecular time; Tennekes and Lumley: more reliable than inertia/viscous ratio because viscous effects act at smaller scales than inertia effects.
sections.teaching_construction: L^2/nu over L/u = Re; the lecture's argument stated as the lecture's reasoning; the judgement attributed, not adopted.

sections.lecture_material: Effective diffusivity K (slide eq. 6); turbulence treated as a fluid property, conceptually dangerous; hypothetical turbulent diffusion process; T ~ L^2/K = Tt gives K ~ uL (slide eqs. 7-8); K/gamma ~ K/nu ~ Re (slide eq. 9); recap of the whole argument.
sections.teaching_construction: K = 0.25 m^2/s for the room; calibration-not-prediction statement.

sections.section: When an eddy diffusivity is a diffusivity
sections.lecture_material: None (motivated by the lecture's 'hypothetical turbulent diffusion process').
sections.research_extension: Taylor 1922 (read 1920): p. 196 quotation; p. 197 heat flux -rho sigma beta [u(x-a)] and [uX] = (1/2) d[X^2]/dt; p. 207 eq. (18) and short-time eq. (19); p. 208 eq. (20) long-time limit with finite integral I.
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of the flux -rho c_p beta <u_p X> from the initial linear temperature and of <u_p X> = (1/2) d<X^2>/dt; derivation of (4.15) through <u_p X> = u^2 int R_L ds with stationarity (R_L depends on the time difference and is even) stated; K(t) = (1/2) d<X^2>/dt from the flux comparison; K = u^2 T_L; exponential-correlation example (4.17) with values at T_L and 10 T_L; Figure 4.1; application to the room (T_L ~ L/u, 10 T_L ~ 1000 s, walls).

sections.research_extension: Standard Atmosphere formulas; Blasius equation in Blasius's variables; coefficient 1.72 of Schubauer and Skramstad.
sections.teaching_construction: NumPy program: air properties at 300 K; room times and ratios with two identity assertions; Blasius RK4 shooting with assertions on the delta* coefficient (1.7208) and on zeta''' <= 0; Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dispersion of 20000 particles asserted against (4.17) within 5 % at t/T_L = 0.1, 1, 10; failure test with the diffusive formula.

sections.section: What the arguments establish and what they do not
sections.teaching_construction: Classification into empirical critical values, derivation (Rayleigh), scale arguments and model (K); stated uncertainties.

sections.lecture_material: Room values; the lecture's critical Reynolds numbers.
sections.research_extension: Exercises 2, 3 and 6 use Schubauer and Skramstad, Meseguer and Trefethen, and Reynolds.
sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises with full solutions, in ascending difficulty: check an assumption, compute, counterexample, derive and compute, judge a model, design and judge.

references.title: Lecture 8 recording
references.supports: Origin of turbulence, critical Reynolds numbers, energy supply, decay, laminarization, spots; diffusivity and the heated room (molecular and turbulent times, buoyancy estimate, 1 cm eddies).

references.title: Lecture 9 recording
references.supports: Time ratio as 1/Pe and 1/Re; Re as a ratio of times (Tennekes and Lumley per the slide); eddy diffusivity K ~ uL and K/nu ~ Re.

references.title: Reynolds 1883, An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine whether the motion of water shall be direct or sinuous (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. 174, 935-982)
references.supports: p. 941: 'fitted with trumpet mouthpieces, so that water might enter without disturbance'. p. 943: U_s = (1/B_s) P/D, B_s = 43.79; 'the critical velocity was very sensitive to disturbance in the water before entering the tubes'; 'the greatest care as to the uniformity of the temperature of the tank and the stillness of the water'; 'the steady motion was unstable for large disturbances long before the critical velocity was reached'; eddies appeared in a 'full-blown manner'. p. 946: a second critical velocity at which existing eddies die out, 'This conclusion has been verified.' p. 948: v_c = (1/278) P/D; 'the ratio being 43.7 to 278'; nature of the surface affects the law of resistance above the critical velocity.
references.page_checked: p. 941 (PDF p. 8); p. 943 (PDF p. 10); p. 946 (PDF p. 13); p. 948 (PDF p. 15); copy at damtp.cam.ac.uk

references.title: Schubauer and Skramstad 1948, Laminar-boundary-layer oscillations and transition on a flat plate (NACA Report 909)
references.supports: p. 1: wave motion with the characteristics predicted by a stability theory based on exponential growth of small disturbances; contributions of Tollmien and Schlichting; stability depends on kinematic viscosity, boundary-layer thickness, outer speed and frequency or wavelength. p. 2: 'transition involves two things'; 'Sufficiently small disturbance cannot produce transition, but a small disturbance may grow according to stability theory until it is sufficiently large to cause the flow to become turbulent'; delta* = 1.72 (nu x/U0)^(1/2) for the Blasius distribution; R = U0 delta*/nu = 1.72 R_x^(1/2). p. 7, Figure 7: effect of turbulence 100 sqrt((u'^2+v'^2+w'^2)/3)/U0 on the x-Reynolds number of transition (read from the graph). p. 30: 'experimentally established lower limit R = 450'; transition delayed until R about 2000; 'If no disturbances were present, theoretically transition should not occur'; 'good agreement with theory'.
references.page_checked: p. 1 (PDF p. 5); p. 2 (PDF p. 6); p. 7 (PDF p. 11); p. 30 (PDF p. 34)

references.title: Meseguer and Trefethen 2003, Linearized pipe flow to Reynolds number 10^7 (J. Comput. Phys. 186, 178-197)
references.supports: p. 1: eigenvalues for R from 10^2 to 10^7. p. 4: R = a U_CL/nu. pp. 10-11: rightmost eigenvalues with negative real parts scaling as R^-1, R^-1/2, R^-1/3 for the modes studied. p. 13: eigenvalues of the operators in question all in the left half-plane. p. 15: 'Transition to turbulence, like turbulence itself, depends on nonlinearity'; L 'itself is eigenvalue stable'; plane Poiseuille eigenvalue instability at R ~ 5772; transition observed at R ~ 350 (plane Couette), 1000 (plane Poiseuille), 2000 (pipe, continued p. 16).
references.page_checked: preprint pp. 1, 4, 10-11, 13, 15-16 (Oxford University Research Archive copy, https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:6f273a01-925c-4862-88a9-9bfe764b5d59); journal pagination not checked

references.title: Darrigol 2002, Stability and instability in nineteenth-century fluid mechanics (Revue d'histoire des mathematiques 8, 5-65)
references.supports: p. 49: Rayleigh 1880 on two-dimensional parallel flow; vorticity equation (19) for inviscid 2D flow; linearization with u, v ~ exp(i(kx - sigma t)). p. 50: stability equation (21) (U - sigma/k)(v'' - k^2 v) - U'' v = 0; multiplication by v* and integration, eqs. (22)-(25); if U'' has constant sign, Im(sigma) = 0; Rayleigh noted the criterion is of no help for the jet, whose U'' changes sign.

references.title: Blasius 1908, The boundary layers in fluids with little friction (NACA TM 1256)
references.supports: TM p. 7: xi = (1/2) sqrt(rho u/k) y/sqrt(x), psi = sqrt(k u/rho) sqrt(x) zeta, u = (1/2) u zeta', zeta zeta'' = -zeta''', zeta(0) = zeta'(0) = 0, zeta'(inf) = 2 (k the viscosity).

references.title: Taylor 1922, Diffusion by continuous movements (Proc. London Math. Soc. (2) 20, 196-212; read 10 June 1920)
references.supports: p. 196: 'turbulent motion is capable of diffusing heat and other diffusible properties through the interior of a fluid in much the same way that molecular agitation gives rise to molecular diffusion'. p. 197: heat conveyed across unit area = -rho sigma beta [u(x-a)]; [u(x-a)] = (1/2) d[X^2]/dt; turbulence uniformly distributed. p. 206: R_xi defined as the correlation of a particle's velocity at an interval xi. p. 207: eq. (18) [X^2] = 2[u^2] int int R_xi; eq. (19) short times. p. 208: lim int R_xi = I finite; eq. (20) [X^2] ~ 2 I T [u^2] at large T.
references.page_checked: pp. 196-197 (PDF pp. 1-2); pp. 206-208 (PDF pp. 11-13); copy at courses.washington.edu

references.title: U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976 (NOAA-S/T 76-1562, NASA-TM-X-74335)
references.page_checked: p. 18 (PDF p. 34); p. 19 (PDF p. 35); p. 20 (PDF p. 36); appended errata note PDF p. 243
